## Introduction

This vignette shows how to solve a simple prediction problem with the
`ridgereg()` function from this package. We use the `BostonHousing` data
from the **mlbench** package and the **caret** package to

1. split the data into a training and a test set,
2. fit a linear regression model and a linear regression model with forward
   selection of covariates,
3. fit ridge regression models with `ridgereg()` for different values of
   $\lambda$ and choose $\lambda$ by 10-fold cross-validation,
4. compare all three models on the test set.

The response is `medv` (median home value in $1000s).

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(AdvancedRlab4)
library(caret)
library(mlbench)
```

## 1. Training and test data

```{r data}
data("BostonHousing")
str(BostonHousing)

set.seed(2024)
train_index <- createDataPartition(BostonHousing$medv, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train <- BostonHousing[train_index, ]
test  <- BostonHousing[-train_index, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

`createDataPartition()` samples within quantile groups of `medv`, so the
response has a similar distribution in both sets.

To make the three models comparable, they all use the same 10 cross-validation
folds of the training set.

```{r folds}
set.seed(2024)
folds <- createFolds(train$medv, k = 10, returnTrain = TRUE)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, index = folds)

x_train <- train[, names(train) != "medv"]
y_train <- train$medv
x_test  <- test[, names(test) != "medv"]
y_test  <- test$medv
```

## 2. Linear regression and forward selection

### Ordinary linear regression

```{r lm}
fit_lm <- train(x = x_train, y = y_train, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
fit_lm
summary(fit_lm)
```

### Linear regression with forward selection

The `leapForward` method in caret tunes `nvmax`, which starts at one
covariate, so it can never select the intercept-only model. Since the forward
selection must be able to choose among models with $0, 1, \dots, n$
covariates, we define a small custom caret model instead. It uses
`stats::step()` with `direction = "forward"`; the tuning parameter `nsteps` is
the number of covariates added, from 0 (intercept only) up to all of them.
Setting `k = 0` removes the AIC penalty so that `step()` always adds the
best remaining covariate until `nsteps` is reached, and cross-validation
(not AIC) decides how many covariates to keep.

```{r forward-model}
forward_lm <- list(
  label = "Linear regression with forward selection",
  library = NULL,
  type = "Regression",
  parameters = data.frame(
    parameter = "nsteps",
    class = "numeric",
    label = "Number of covariates"
  ),
  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
    data.frame(nsteps = 0:ncol(x))
  },
  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, weights, classProbs, ...) {
    dat <- as.data.frame(x)
    dat$.outcome <- y
    upper <- reformulate(names(x), response = ".outcome")
    start <- lm(.outcome ~ 1, data = dat)
    step(
      start,
      scope = list(lower = ~ 1, upper = upper),
      direction = "forward",
      steps = param$nsteps,
      k = 0,
      trace = 0
    )
  },
  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
    predict(modelFit, newdata = as.data.frame(newdata))
  },
  prob = NULL,
  sort = function(x) x[order(x$nsteps), ]
)
```

```{r forward-fit}
p <- ncol(x_train)

fit_fwd <- train(
  x = x_train, y = y_train,
  method = forward_lm,
  tuneGrid = data.frame(nsteps = 0:p),
  trControl = ctrl
)
fit_fwd
```

The tuning grid contains all `r p + 1` candidates (0 to `r p` covariates), so
the condition on the model search is satisfied. The cross-validated RMSE
for each model size:

```{r forward-plot}
plot(fit_fwd, xlab = "Number of covariates")
fit_fwd$bestTune
summary(fit_fwd$finalModel)
```

## 3. Performance on the training set

```{r train-perf}
perf <- function(model, x, y) {
  postResample(pred = predict(model, newdata = x), obs = y)
}

train_perf <- rbind(
  `Linear regression`  = perf(fit_lm,  x_train, y_train),
  `Forward selection`  = perf(fit_fwd, x_train, y_train)
)
round(train_perf, 3)
```

The training error is optimistic, since the same data were used to fit the
models. The cross-validated estimates above are more honest about
out-of-sample performance.

## 4. Ridge regression with ridgereg()

To use `ridgereg()` in caret we define a custom model, as described in the
caret documentation. It has one tuning parameter, `lambda`. caret passes the
predictors `x` and outcome `y` separately, so `fit` first combines them into a
data frame and then calls `ridgereg()`. `ridgereg()` standardizes the
predictors internally and `predict.ridgereg()` applies the same scaling to new
data.

```{r ridge-model}
ridge_caret <- list(
  label = "Ridge regression (ridgereg)",
  library = NULL,
  type = "Regression",
  parameters = data.frame(
    parameter = "lambda",
    class = "numeric",
    label = "Lambda"
  ),
  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
    data.frame(lambda = 10^seq(-3, 3, length.out = len))
  },
  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, weights, classProbs, ...) {
    dat <- as.data.frame(x)
    dat$.outcome <- y
    ridgereg(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, lambda = param$lambda)
  },
  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, submodels = NULL) {
    predict(modelFit, newdata = as.data.frame(newdata))
  },
  prob = NULL,
  sort = function(x) x[order(-x$lambda), ]
)
```

## 5. Choosing lambda by 10-fold cross-validation

We evaluate a grid of $\lambda$ values on a logarithmic scale (plus
$\lambda = 0$, which corresponds to ordinary least squares) using the same
folds as before.

```{r ridge-fit}
lambda_grid <- data.frame(lambda = c(0, 10^seq(-3, 3, length.out = 40)))

fit_ridge <- train(
  x = x_train, y = y_train,
  method = ridge_caret,
  tuneGrid = lambda_grid,
  trControl = ctrl
)

fit_ridge$bestTune
```

```{r ridge-plot}
plot(fit_ridge, scales = list(x = list(log = 10)))
```

The cross-validated RMSE for the best $\lambda$ and its neighbours:

```{r ridge-results}
res <- fit_ridge$results
res <- res[order(res$RMSE), ]
head(res[, c("lambda", "RMSE", "Rsquared", "MAE")], 5)
```

The final model, refitted by caret on the whole training set with the
selected $\lambda$, is

```{r ridge-final}
fit_ridge$finalModel
```

## 6. Evaluation on the test set

```{r test-perf}
test_perf <- rbind(
  `Linear regression`          = perf(fit_lm,    x_test, y_test),
  `Forward selection`          = perf(fit_fwd,   x_test, y_test),
  `Ridge regression (ridgereg)` = perf(fit_ridge, x_test, y_test)
)
round(test_perf, 3)
```

```{r test-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
models <- list(`Linear` = fit_lm, `Forward` = fit_fwd, `Ridge` = fit_ridge)
for (nm in names(models)) {
  pred <- predict(models[[nm]], newdata = x_test)
  plot(y_test, pred, xlab = "Observed medv", ylab = "Predicted medv",
       main = nm, pch = 1)
  abline(0, 1, col = "red")
}
par(oldpar)
```

### Concluding comments

```{r conclusion-helper, echo = FALSE}
best <- rownames(test_perf)[which.min(test_perf[, "RMSE"])]
```

On the test set the model with the lowest RMSE is **`r best`**
(RMSE = `r round(min(test_perf[, "RMSE"]), 3)`).

Some points to keep in mind when interpreting the results:

- The Boston housing data has 13 predictors and about 500 observations, and
  some predictors are correlated (for example `tax` and `rad`). Ridge
  regression is designed for this situation, but with this many observations
  per covariate the benefit over ordinary least squares is usually small,
  and the three test errors are expected to be close to each other.
- Forward selection typically keeps most of the covariates here. The
  cross-validation curve flattens after a handful of predictors, so the
  chosen model size is not very sharply determined.
- The best $\lambda$ is chosen on the training set only, so the test set gives
  an unbiased comparison. Because the test set is small (about 100 rows),
  differences of a few hundredths in RMSE are within noise; a different
  random split could change the ranking.
- All three models are linear in the predictors. The residual patterns in
  the diagnostic plots (see `plot.linreg()`) suggest non-linear effects, for
  example in `lstat`, so a more flexible model would likely improve
  predictions more than any choice among these three.
